paper.title_en: Dark matter or tidal charge? Degeneracies in rotating black-hole images
paper.abstract_en: A black-hole image can differ from Kerr for more than one reason. Matter around the hole can bend photon paths, while an effective correction to the spacetime can leave a similar imprint. We compare phenomenological Einasto and cored Navarro--Frenk--White dark-matter dressings with a rotating braneworld geometry carrying negative tidal charge. The tidal charge is profiled against photon-region observables and smooth image measures across three spins, four inclinations, three dark-matter amplitudes, two halo families, and three weighting choices. With the reference $1\%$ photon and $5\%$ image scales, all 72 dark-matter configurations admit an interior negative-$q$ mimic. The overlap is broad but not exact: it weakens near $a/M=0.95$ and becomes more fragile when the photon and image blocks receive equal weight. A first Fourier-space test gives nearly identical normalized visibility amplitudes at the reference point, with a larger residual at high spin. Changing the halo shape shifts the best-fit charge but does not remove the matched branch. A ray-bundle caustic test fails the required topology check and is therefore excluded from inference. Current EHT shadow-size constraints remain too weak to separate the branches, while local zero-angular-momentum-observer escape cones retain small but well-resolved differences. Distinct radial corrections can therefore occupy nearly the same distant observable manifold. The boundaries of this overlap point to high spin, phase-sensitive interferometry, and local photon transport as the most promising discriminants.
